text:
maria: Heads-up — I'm seeing a big mismatch between our synthetic runner and the replay harness on the KV-cache microbench. Synthetic shows 8–12ms p99, replay shows 40–80ms tails. Suspect client-side connection behavior. :eyes:

ajay: Can you paste the harness config? My first guess is connection churn + TLS handshakes. Replay might be opening a lot of short-lived HTTP/1.1 connections. gRPC should be persistent http2 streams, right?

maria: Replay is the 'session-replay' harness that tries to mimic prod traffic; it replays recorded sessions so it re-opens connections per user session. Synthetic bench uses long-lived pooled connections. Here's the client flags we used in the replay harness:

```
--concurrency=200 \n--session-duration-ms=1500 \n--use-http1=true \n--tls-verify=true
```

kevin: yup, that's going to blow up TLS and socket churn. Also check TCP_NODELAY and SO_KEEPALIVE. If Nagle is on you get delayed small writes; if clients open/close sockets quickly you'll get extra retransmits and delayed acks.

lina: quick data point: I attached a perf map from one replay run — most CPU is in kernel on accept/close and in openssl_handshake. The runtime-side user CPU is low. So it smells like syscall/tls overhead, not model runtime. :face_with_monocle:

bench-bot: snapshot metrics (replay-run-2026-09-14): connections/sec=450, avg-conn-duration=1.8s, TLS-handshakes/sec=430, tcp_retransmits=12/s, accept_recv_cpu_pct=38%

ajay: That's consistent. Two quick experiments to isolate: 1) force long-lived connections in replay (keepalive + reuse) and 2) run same trace but use http2/gRPC client so we avoid frequent TLS. If p99 drops, it's client-side artifact.

maria: tried #1: set keepalive on the replay runner (SO_KEEPALIVE + keepalive_time=60) and enabled connection pooling — p99 dropped from 72ms -> 14ms. Batches behaving better too (less fragmentation of requests across kernels).

kevin: nice. Also try disabling Nagle (TCP_NODELAY=1) on short RPCs — that often helps for small chatty RPCs. But beware: if you also enable batching in runtime, TCP_NODELAY might reduce batching efficiency. It's a trade-off.

lina: note about gRPC vs REST: gRPC (HTTP/2) multiplexes many streams over one connection so it amortizes TLS and TCP costs — but pressure on server-side socket threads/change in kernel scheduling can show up as head-of-line effects for very long sequences. We saw one perf regression where switching a default kernel selector caused 30% higher syscall time under heavy HTTP/2 multiplexing.

ajay: Important benchmarking hygiene: 1) warm KV cache (measure cold vs warm explicitly), 2) align client connection model (pooling vs churn) between harnesses, 3) run with and without TLS resumption (session tickets) to measure handshake amortization, 4) instrument kernel vs user time and syscall counts, 5) check for epoll vs io_uring differences on test boxes.

maria: Agreed. Action items: - I'll add a flag to the replay harness to optionally reuse connections and toggle http2/grpc mode. - Lina, can you re-run the perf profile with SO_KEEPALIVE off/on and TCP_NODELAY toggles? - Ajay, can you add a dashboard comparing TLS-handshakes/sec vs p99 latency so we can see correlation?

ajay: on it. Also we should capture a small client-only synthetic that opens N connections with short sessions to reproduce the worst-case — we can run it on a separate node and ensure it's not the server workload causing artifacts.

kevin: one last gotcha we hit before: load generators with many concurrent short connects can saturate ephemeral port range or hit SYN backlog limits. Make sure ephemeral_port range and net.ipv4.tcp_max_syn_backlog are tuned, or you'll see clients timeout which inflates p99 massively.

maria: Good point — adding ephemeral port and backlog checks to the runbook. OK let's reconvene after the two re-runs. Thanks all :thumbsup:
